chunks.st: If a wall between two courtyards

chunks.st: If there was produce on top of the wall,

chunks.en: as long as they do not bring it down.
chunks.st: provided that they do not lower the produce down from on top of the wall to one of the courtyards.

chunks.en: If the wall broke open up to ten amos,
chunks.st: If the wall was breached, the following distinction applies: If the breach was up to ten cubits wide,

chunks.st: they establish one eiruv, and they may not establish two, as a breach of this size nullifies the partition and joins the two courtyards into a single domain.

summary: If a board four tefachim wide is put across the ditch, or between two balconies, the courtyards may make one eiruv together if they want. A thinner board does not join them.

summary: A pile of hay ten tefachim tall between two courtyards is like a wall. Both sides may feed their animals from it. If the hay gets lower than ten tefachim, they make one eiruv.

chunks.en: A pile of hay between two courtyards,
chunks.st: With regard to a haystack that is positioned between two courtyards

chunks.en: ten tefachim tall,
chunks.st: and is ten handbreadths high,
chunks.stMore: it has the status of a partition,

chunks.en: they make two eiruvin and may not make one.
chunks.st: and therefore the residents of the courtyards may establish two eiruvin, and they may not establish one eiruv.

chunks.he: אֵלּוּ מַאֲכִילִין מִכָּאן וְאֵלּוּ מַאֲכִילִין מִכָּאן.
chunks.en: These feed their animals from here, and those feed from there.
chunks.st: These, the inhabitants of one courtyard, may feed their animals from here, from one side of the haystack, and those, the inhabitants of the other courtyard, may feed their animals from there, from the other side of the haystack.
chunks.stMore: There is no concern that the haystack might become too small to serve as a partition.

chunks.en: If the hay became lower than ten tefachim,
chunks.st: If the height of the hay was reduced to less than ten handbreadths
chunks.stMore: across its entire length, its legal status is no longer that of a partition. Consequently,

chunks.en: they make one eiruv and may not make two.
chunks.st: the residents of both courtyards establish one eiruv, and they do not establish two eiruvin.

summary: How does one person make a shituf for everyone in the alleyway? He puts down a barrel of his food and gives it to them through someone else who can take it for them.

chunks.en: How do we make a shituf in an alleyway?
chunks.st: How does one merge the courtyards that open into the alleyway,
chunks.stMore: if a person wishes to act on behalf of all the residents of the alleyway?

chunks.en: He puts down the barrel and says,
chunks.st: He places a barrel filled with his own food and says:

chunks.en: This is for all the people of the alleyway.
chunks.st: This is for all the residents of the alleyway.
chunks.stMore: For this gift to be acquired by the others, someone must accept it on their behalf,

chunks.en: And he gives it to them through his son
chunks.st: and the tanna therefore teaches that he may confer possession to them

chunks.en: and daughter who are grown up, and through his servant
chunks.st: even by means of his adult son or daughter, and

chunks.en: and maid who are Jewish, and through his wife.
chunks.st: likewise by means of his Hebrew slave or maidservant, whom he does not own, and by means of his wife.
chunks.stMore: These people may acquire the eiruv on behalf of all the residents of the alleyway.

chunks.en: But he may not give it to them
chunks.st: However, he may not confer possession

chunks.en: through his son and daughter who are young, nor
chunks.st: by means of his minor son or daughter, nor

chunks.en: through his non-Jewish servant and maid,
chunks.st: by means of his Canaanite slave or maidservant,

chunks.en: because their hand is like his hand.
chunks.explain: What they get belongs to him, so it is as if he never gave it away.
chunks.st: because they cannot effect acquisition, as ownership of objects that come into their possession is as if those objects came into his possession. Consequently, the master or father cannot confer possession to the slave or minor respectively on behalf of others as their acquisition is ineffective and the object remains in his own possession.

chunks.en: and he must tell them.
chunks.st: to them, and he must inform the new residents of their inclusion in the merging of alleyways.

chunks.st: However, with regard to the remnants of an eiruv,

summary: Rabbi Eliezer says an eiruv may be made with any food except water and salt. Rabbi Yehoshua says it must be a whole loaf; even a small whole loaf works, but a big loaf in pieces does not.

chunks.en: We may make an eiruv and a shituf with any food,
chunks.st: One may join courtyards and merge alleyways with all types of food,

chunks.en: we may not make an eiruv with it.

summary: May a person pay a storekeeper so that he will get a share in the eiruv? The Rabbis argue. Rabbi Yehudah says a courtyard eiruv may be made for someone without asking him, because it only helps him.

chunks.en: A person may give a coin to a storekeeper or a baker
chunks.st: A person may give a ma’a coin to a grocer or a baker,
chunks.stMore: if they live in the same alleyway or courtyard,

chunks.en: so that he will get a share in the eiruv for him,
chunks.st: so that the grocer or baker will confer upon him possession of wine or bread for a merging of the alleyway or an eiruv,
chunks.stMore: if other residents come to them to purchase these products for that purpose.

chunks.en: says Rabbi Eliezer.
chunks.st: This is the statement of Rabbi Eliezer.

chunks.en: But the Sages say,
chunks.st: And the Rabbis say:

chunks.en: his money did not get it for him.
chunks.st: His money did not confer possession on him,
chunks.stMore: as the transfer of money alone is not a valid mode of acquisition and cannot confer possession. One must perform a valid mode of acquisition, e.g., pulling an article into one’s possession, to transfer ownership.

chunks.en: And they agree about all other people
chunks.st: And the Rabbis concede with regard to all other people,
chunks.stMore: apart from grocers and bakers,

chunks.en: that his money does get it for him,
chunks.st: that if one gave them money for the food of an eiruv, his money confers possession upon him,

chunks.en: because we only make an eiruv for a person when he knows.
chunks.st: as one may establish an eiruv for a person only with his knowledge
chunks.stMore: and at his bidding. With regard to a grocer or baker, the person giving the money does not intend to appoint the grocer or the baker as his agent and the money itself does not effect an acquisition, and consequently, he did not accomplish anything. With regard to anyone else, however, there is no doubt that he must have intended to appoint him his agent, and his act is effective.

chunks.en: Rabbi Yehudah said,
chunks.st: Rabbi Yehuda said:

chunks.en: when does this apply?
chunks.st: In what case is this statement said?

chunks.en: For an eiruv techumin.
chunks.st: It is said with regard to a joining of Shabbat boundaries,

words.note: An eiruv that lets us walk farther than 2000 amos.

chunks.en: But for an eiruv for courtyards,
chunks.st: but with regard to a joining of courtyards, one

chunks.en: we may make it for him whether he knows or not,
chunks.st: may establish an eiruv for a person either with his knowledge or without his knowledge.

chunks.en: because we may do something good for a person when he is not there,
chunks.st: The reason is because one may act for a person’s benefit in his absence,

chunks.en: but we may not do something bad for a person when he is not there.
chunks.explain: An eiruv techumin lets him walk one way but takes away the other way.
chunks.st: but one may not act to a person’s disadvantage in his absence. As a participant in a joining of courtyards benefits from his inclusion in the eiruv, his consent is not required. However, with regard to a joining of Shabbat boundaries, although it enables one to go farther in one direction, he loses the option of traveling in the opposite direction. When an action is to a person’s disadvantage, or if it entails both benefits and disadvantages, one may act on that person’s behalf only if he has been explicitly appointed his agent.
